title: Choosing scissors for needlework
subtitle: What to look for in embroidery scissors and when to reach for which pair.
excerpt: Needlework uses at least two pairs of scissors: sharp thread snippers for cutting floss close to the fabric, and fabric shears for cutting cloth. Using the wrong pair damages the blade. This reading covers what each type does and how to care for them.
sourceNotes: Tool selection guidance synthesised from contemporary needlework practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small, fine-pointed scissors used specifically for cutting thread and trimming stitches close to the fabric surface. The pointed tips allow precise cutting in tight spaces. Not used for cutting fabric.

content.text: are the tool needleworkers reach for most often. Keeping the right pair to hand and using it only for its intended purpose makes the work easier and keeps the blades sharp.

Thread snippers are spring-loaded and cut with a squeeze rather than a traditional open-and-close action. They clip thread with one hand while the other holds the work. Use them for cutting thread ends close to the cloth, for trimming tails behind the hoop, and for quick cuts mid-stitch.

Fine-pointed embroidery scissors have a sharp tip that can enter tight spaces and snip a single stitch without cutting the fabric. Use these for removing stitches and for trimming close to finished work. Look for blades around 5 to 7 cm long with a clean meet at the tip.

Fabric shears are large scissors with long blades, used only for cutting cloth. Using them on thread or paper dulls the edge quickly. Keep them separate from thread scissors and mark them clearly so other household members don't use them for crafts or kitchen work.

Wipe the blades after each session to remove fibre residue. Store with the tips protected, either in a needle case or with a tip cover. Sharpen embroidery scissors at a proper sharpener; household sharpening kits rarely work on fine points.
